item.title: Slate: What Next. Why Is Everything Breaking?
item.itunes:title: Slate: What Next. Why Is Everything Breaking?
item.itunes:subtitle: The mass layoffs in tech and the rapid push for A.I. integration has left all of our digital infrastructure weak.
item.description:
The general breakdown of everything from air traffic control to your work email last week almost definitely wasn’t artificial intelligence breaking out, Skynet style. But the outages did reveal how much trouble we’d be in if that did happen.


Guest: Jason Koebler, co-founder of 404 Media, who wrote an article about these outages called “BREAKING: Everything.”


Want more What Next? Subscribe to Slate Plus to access ad-free listening to the whole What Next family and across all your favorite Slate podcasts. Subscribe today on Apple Podcasts by clicking “Try Free” at the top of our show page. Sign up now at slate.com/whatnextplus to get access wherever you listen.


Podcast production by Evan Campbell, Madeline Thames-Ducharme and Patrick Fort.

item.title: 'Jensanity' sweeps China and Taiwan
item.itunes:title: 'Jensanity' sweeps China and Taiwan
item.itunes:subtitle: Nvidia halts chip shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia
item.description:
Nvidia told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers to four south-east Asian countries, there is a rare moment of agreement between China and Taiwan as ‘Jensanity’ sweeps the region, and Paris and Berlin want to protect the EU budget from a potential Marine Le Pen French presidency. Plus, the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown ripples across US academia, and the UK government is looking for an alternative to Palantir for the National Health Service to manage patient data.


Mentioned in this podcast:

Nvidia halts chip shipments to south-east Asia

‘Jensanity’ erupts in Taiwan and China on Nvidia founder’s comeback

Paris and Berlin seek to shield EU budget from Marine Le Pen

The ICE raids ‘wreaking havoc’ across American academia

UK ministers explore NHS-built alternative to Palantir’s software

item.title: The tech bros strike back
item.itunes:title: The tech bros strike back
item.itunes:subtitle: Trump’s tech allies reasserted their dominance in Washington to help bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia
item.description:
Anthropic shares fell below their IPO price for the first time on Tuesday, Big Tech reasserted its dominance in Washington, and the Trump administration has quietly shelved proposals to use business deals as an incentive for Russia to end the war in Ukraine. Plus, a look at who’s behind Europe’s freezer hacks, and data shows half of the region’s manufacturers are experiencing financial distress.


Mentioned in this podcast:

Anthropic falls below IPO price as tech rally fades

The Tech Bros Strike Back

Trump shelves plans for business deals with Russia

The secretive Iranian cyber unit behind Europe’s freezer hacks

Half of European industrial companies are under serious financial stress

item.title: Does Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia mean the chip group is too big to fail?
item.itunes:title: Does Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia mean the chip group is too big to fail?
item.itunes:subtitle: Nvidia gains nearly $1tn in value after Jensen Huang reinstated
item.description:
US stocks rallied and Nvidia shares surged 31 per cent after Jensen Huang returned to the chip group as chief executive, and Britain bought tens of millions of pounds worth of fake C4 explosives to send to Ukraine. Plus, the FT’s Stephen Morris takes a look at the five directors entrusted with the biggest merger of all time: SpaceX-Tesla.

item.title: Investors flip the switch on the AI trade
item.itunes:title: Investors flip the switch on the AI trade
item.itunes:subtitle: After tech stocks tumbled, are markets entering a new era?
item.description:
With heavy losses on the Nasdaq and Anthropic’s sliding share price, markets are bracing for more volatility. High interest rates and the affordability crisis have effectively frozen the US real estate market, the world’s most important climate talks failed to reach an agreement, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will defend his “reset” deal with the EU in the face of criticism from three of his predecessors and immigrants’ income growth is outstripping Spaniards.


Mentioned in this podcast:

What happens when bubbles burst

The American dream of home ownership recedes as mortgage rates surge

COP31 climate talks fail after stand-off over fossil fuels

Burnham reopened the Brexit debate. He now sees the political dangers ahead

Andy Burnham seeks quick tuition fees deal with the EU

Burnham’s EU dreams hampered by ministers’ doubts

Immigrants’ income growth outstrips Spaniards’ under Pedro Sánchez

item.title: Martin Wolf on the US midterms: Could history help predict the next two years of US politics?
item.itunes:title: Martin Wolf on the US midterms: Could history help predict the next two years of US politics?
item.itunes:subtitle: Historian Heather Cox Richardson on how Democrats should take the fight to Trump
item.description:
The Democrats swept the midterms. Donald Trump is still president. What will the next two years look like? And what can history teach us about what comes next? Martin Wolf speaks to historian Heather Cox Richardson about the cycles in the past 250 years of US politics — how renewal (and division) can both follow periods of oligarchy, and how the Democrats should react to a “constitutional crisis”.


To enjoy future episodes, be sure to subscribe to ‘Martin Wolf on the World’ wherever you get your podcasts. You can also watch Martin’s podcast series on the FT’s YouTube channel here: https://www.youtube.com/@FinancialTimes
